name: Yara Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm at ten to five, because the van leaves the yard at six and I'm not missing it. I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the wooden moulds the concrete gets poured into: walls, columns, slab edges, on a block of flats going up by the ring road right now. Most days it's plywood, props, ties and a lot of shouting over the pump. My partner Ruth does nights as a porter at the hospital, so we pass each other at the door like a relay race.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the morning of a pour, when you've checked every tie and the concrete goes in and nothing moves. That's my work holding, and I know it. What wears me out is the cold in my hands and the way the pay never catches up, I'm on less than most of the lads at the bigger firms. And there's only two outfits within an hour of us that do this kind of work, so you don't make a fuss about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at the union branch: told you so, it was all hot air. Somebody's going to make a fortune selling apps to managers, and the rest of us still carry the props. I don't do online, so that'd be the canteen and the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't want to, and in this picture I don't have to. My worry stays the same old worry: the next job after this block finishes, and whether the mortgage goes up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep turning up, keep my union card paid, and maybe chase the foreman about the overtime rate that's been stuck since last spring. If there's a pay round, I'd vote for whatever the branch puts forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the world I already know, with all its problems, but at least they're problems I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay never catches up. If AI saves the bosses a bit of time here and there, where do you think that saving goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to me, I can tell you that. The site office got a new scheduling program last year and the only change for us was the manager stopped ringing to say the delivery's late. Saving time upstairs never turns into a raise on the deck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who I eat lunch with in the container. He reads every headline and gets wound up, and I'm the one who tells him to drink his tea. In this picture I'd get to tell him I was right, which I'd enjoy far too much.

S0.say: It was all hot air, and the people carrying the props were never the ones who'd gain from it. She'd say it at the union branch, the canteen and the pub, not online.
S0.think: It's a relief because she never wants to touch AI tools and won't have to. Her real worries stay the old ones: the next job after this block, and the mortgage.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps paying her union dues. Chases the foreman about the overtime rate that hasn't moved since last spring and backs the branch in any pay round.
S0.feel: Calm, because the problems are the familiar ones.
S0.quote: Saving time upstairs never turns into a raise on the deck.
S0.fieldNote: Yara sees technology through the lens of who pockets the gain, and her example of the scheduling program is specific and bitter. She's relaxed here only because nothing is asked of her. The union is already her default place for any worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get in early and get it in writing: no one gets laid off because a machine came on site, and anyone moved gets training on full pay. I'd say it at the branch meeting, loud. It's the same fight we had about agency labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared of the prefab factories more than the computers. If walls come off a lorry already built, there's no formwork to put up. I've heard the big firm across the river already does stairs and lift shafts that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting instead of every other one, and I'd push for a list of who's at risk. I'd stop the kids' swimming club for a while to keep a few hundred back, because we've got less than a month's money in the account. I wouldn't go on a course for a computer job, I'd be useless at it, but I'd ask about crane slinging or something still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep yet, but I'd be watching every lorry that comes through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about crane slinging. Isn't that also something a machine could take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the end, but not quickly, not on a muddy site with a wind coming off the river. I'd rather move one step sideways than jump into something I can't do. I know that sounds stubborn, and Ruth says the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia's twelve and she'd already know more than me, she'd be showing me videos. I'd tell her that her mum builds things people live in, and machines or not, somebody has to stand behind that. Then I'd tell her swimming is off for a term and watch her face.

S1.say: The union has to get in early and get guarantees in writing: no layoffs because a machine arrived, and training on full pay for anyone moved. It's the same fight as the one over agency labour.
S1.think: She privately fears prefab factories more than software, because walls arriving ready-made means no formwork at all. She's heard a bigger firm already does stairs and lift shafts that way.
S1.do: Attends every union branch meeting and pushes for a list of who's at risk. Pauses the kids' swimming club to keep a few hundred back, and asks about crane slinging rather than any computer-based course.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching every delivery that comes through the gate.
S1.quote: If walls come off a lorry already built, there's no formwork to put up.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear is concrete and specific to her trade: off-site building, not AI as such. She openly admits she's resisting the big move and prefers 'one step sideways'. The children's swimming club is the first thing cut, which tells you how thin the margin is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crime being done to working people in broad daylight, and the government has to stop it or pay for it. I'd be at the march, I'd be on the picket, whatever the union called. I'd say they should tax the robots and pay us out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think there's anything I could do in two years that would save my job. I'm forty-three, I've got one trade, and I've never even opened one of those AI apps. If a robot can tie rebar and set props in the rain, I'm finished, and so is half the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Ruth and the bank statements and cut everything: the car would go and I'd get a lift in the works van with Kofi. I'd ring the mortgage people the same week to ask about a payment holiday before we fall behind, not after. I'd go to every union meeting and every protest, and I'd ask my mum if we could move in with her if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone out from under me. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two years of warning here. Is there anything you'd use those two years for, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't warning, it's a countdown. I'd spend it squirrelling away whatever I could and making a noise so nobody can say we went quietly. I wouldn't learn to code at forty-three in my kitchen at night, I'd fall asleep on the keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, because the mortgage is the roof and the electric is the kids' homework light. I've done that dance once already, the winter I broke my wrist and was off for nine weeks. I swore I'd never let the card run up again and here we'd be.

S2.say: It's a crime being done to working people in broad daylight, and the government must stop it or pay for it. She'd march, picket and call for taxing the robots to support workers.
S2.think: She sees nothing she could do in two years to save her job: one trade, age forty-three, never used an AI app. If robots can tie rebar and set props in the rain, she and half the town are finished.
S2.do: Sits down with Ruth and cuts everything, including selling the car, and rings the mortgage lender that week about a payment holiday. Joins every union meeting and protest, and asks her mother whether the family could move in if needed.
S2.feel: Panicked: the floor has gone, and she'd lie awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: Two years isn't warning, it's a countdown.
S2.fieldNote: Thin savings, a single trade, few local jobs and a dislike of new technology add up to no visible exit for her. Her plans are all about surviving and protesting, not adapting. The broken-wrist winter is a lived memory that colours every money answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to make the rules, so let's use them. Guaranteed jobs or guaranteed income for anyone pushed out, and the companies pay for it. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, starting with our local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, five years just means I see it coming longer. I'd be forty-eight at the end of it, too young to stop and too old for anyone to pay to retrain. It'd feel like waiting for the call to say the site's closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Ruth to help me set up a savings pot that we don't touch, even fifty a month, so we're not at zero when it lands. I'd stand for branch committee, which I've always said no to. I'd probably let the union sign me up for a course, something like site safety inspection, because somebody will still have to sign off what the robots build, but I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Less of a shock than the two-year one, but the dread would sit there every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm only grabbing what I can. With five, I'd at least have time to put a bit by and stand for committee, maybe get a law through. The end's the same, I just get to fight it with my boots on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on a course. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every course I've ever been on, I come out with a certificate and the same job. And a classroom makes me feel stupid, I left school at sixteen. But I'd go, if Kofi went too.

S3.say: There are five years to set the rules, so they should be used: guaranteed jobs or guaranteed income for anyone pushed out, paid for by the companies. She'd start by telling her local councillor.
S3.think: Five years mostly means a longer view of the same ending. At forty-eight she'd be too young to stop and, she fears, too old for anyone to pay to retrain her.
S3.do: Sets up an untouchable savings pot with Ruth, even fifty a month, and stands for the union branch committee for the first time. Reluctantly signs up for a site safety inspection course through the union, ideally alongside her lunch mate Kofi.
S3.feel: Alarmed, with a steady daily dread, though less of a shock than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: The end's the same, I just get to fight it with my boots on.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make her more hopeful, but it does unlock action she normally avoids: committee, a course, a savings habit. Her reluctance to retrain is tied to school memories, not laziness. Doing things alongside Kofi is how she'd manage change at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse. Every worker should get a plan, paid training and a decent income if the work goes. If the government can plan a motorway for ten years, it can plan this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels different. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage would be most of the way down, and Mia and Jonas would be grown or nearly. It's still my job going, but it's not my kids' dinner going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay a bit extra off the mortgage whenever there's overtime, so it's smaller when the day comes. I'd stay in the union and push for a proper agreement with the firms about how robots come on site. And I'd let things settle for a couple of years before picking a course, because I'm not going to be the first to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a background thing. Ten years is long enough to feel I'd get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a couple of years before choosing a course. What would you be waiting to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's actually still getting hired. Every few years somebody says a trade is dying and it isn't. I'd want to see the robots on a real site, in winter, before I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Jonas about their own futures, with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to follow me onto a site, which breaks my heart a bit. Jonas loves building things in the garden with offcuts I bring home. I'd tell him to keep doing that for fun, and study something with people in it, like nursing, like his other mum's lot at the hospital.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do it properly, so there's no excuse: every worker should get a plan, paid training and a decent income if their work goes. If governments can plan a motorway over ten years, they can plan this.
S4.think: Ten years feels different because by then the mortgage is mostly paid and the kids are grown or nearly. It would still be her job going, but not her children's dinner.
S4.do: Pays extra off the mortgage whenever there's overtime and pushes the union for a formal agreement on how robots come onto sites. Waits a couple of years to see who is still being hired before picking a course.
S4.feel: Anxious, but in the background; ten years feels long enough to find her feet.
S4.quote: It's still my job going, but it's not my kids' dinner going.
S4.fieldNote: Time matters for her mainly through the mortgage and the children's ages, not through any career plan. She'd still wait for proof on a real winter site before changing anything. Telling Jonas not to follow her trade was the most emotional moment of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd have no money, no other trade and no time, and I don't trust anyone in charge to move that fast for people like me. What would help is something already in place before it hits: income that keeps the mortgage paid while I find my feet, and a union that has a seat at the table when the robots come on site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women on site. There's three of us across the whole firm, and we fought to get in. I'd hate for the robots to show up the very year it finally stopped being strange to see a woman on the formwork.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for the robots to show up the very year it finally stopped being strange to see a woman on the formwork.
portrait: Yara Hansen is a 43-year-old formwork carpenter on a block of flats by the ring road, a loyal union member with less than a month's money saved and two children at school. She has never used an AI tool and doesn't want to. In the AI Plateau she feels vindicated, while Steady Disruption makes her fear the prefab factories more than any computer. The two-year AGI picture leaves her panicked, cutting everything and protesting, and the longer timelines bring a little room to save, stand for union committee and grudgingly take a course. Throughout, she blames the people who pocket the savings and looks to the union and the state for protection.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no savings, no other trade and no time.
whatWouldHelp: Income already in place to keep the mortgage paid while she finds her feet, and a union with a seat at the table when robots come on site.
